content:
Theoretical Scenario

At the completion of a course, participants are given a survey of 10 questions. To perform the survey, participants access a URL in their web browser that is made available for a short period of time and requires that students log in with their username and password for the organization.

The beginning of the survey prompts for the name of the course, but not their name. Instead, the survey description on this page indicates that all answers and the survey itself will remain anonymous.

Executive management wishes to use the results of the survey to determine which courses require redesign or updating. You are the data analyst assigned to this task and are required to provide actionable insights for this purpose to executive management.

The first question on the survey is shown here:

Figure 1: Example of the first course evaluation question.

Some ethics concepts and terms that may be discussed here include: • Privacy • Anonymity • Informed Consent • Accountability • Data Minimization • Transparency • Fairness • Bias • Trust

  1. Based on the information provided, what ethical issues are apparent in the design of this survey and in the sample question?

a. False Anonymity

Participants needed to use their credentials to log in, yet the survey claimed to be anonymous.

• Would the system truly be anonymous? • Where is the login information stored? • Would it be possible to link responses back to individuals?

This could be very misleading and violates participant trust.

b. Lack of Transparency

The participants are never told:

• What data is being collected. • Who has access to it. • The length of time it will be stored. • If their login information is retained. Participants can’t provide proper informed consent if this information isn’t presented. c. Potential for Response Bias

Students may fear negative outcomes if they criticize a course.

This could cause:

• Inflated ratings • Untruthful responses • Lack of clarity and usefulness in the data

d. Design Bias in the Survey

The questions could be worded in a way that responses could unintentionally steer participants towards certain answers.

Using poorly designed questions like this can lead to misleading data collection.

  1. What other ethical issues could be present for this survey?

a. Data Security

• How is the data from the survey stored? • Is it properly encrypted? • Who has access to the data? • What data is being recorded? If security is weak and more data than needed is collected, personal information could easily be exposed. b. Function Creep

The data that is collected could potentially be used to:

• Instructor evaluations • Track student performance • Review employee performance Using data beyond its original intent without consent is unethical. c. Re-Identification Risk

Even without names, combinations of information could identify the participants.

• Course name • Submission time • Class size • Demographic information It can be difficult to guarantee true anonymity.

d. Lack of Data Retention Policies

• No indication of how long the data will be stored • No indication of when it will be deleted • No indication of who will be responsible for deleting it

  1. What recommendations would you make to executive management?

a. Be Truthful About Anonymity Do not claim that the survey is anonymous unless it is technically impossible to identify the participants. b. Improve Transparency Provide a clear privacy statement that explains: • What data is collected • Why this data is collected • Who will have access to it • How long it will be stored

c. Separate Authentication from Responses

Login only verifies eligibility; once verified, the user’s identity is immediately decoupled from their answers.

d. Limit Access

A very limited number of authorized personnel should have access to the survey’s raw data.

e. Establish Retention Policies

Define:

• How long is data stored? • When will it be deleted? • Procedures for secure deletion

f. Report Aggregated Data Results Provide summaries instead of individual responses. For example: 92% of the students felt that the course material was current and up to date. This is better than exposing individual answers. 4. If executive management rejects your recommendations and insists there are no issues, how could you proceed ethically?

a. Document Your Recommendations and Concerns

Keep written records of:

• Identified risks • Recommendations provided • Concerns and your reasons for them This demonstrates professional due diligence. b. Escalate Concerns if Necessary

Speak with:

• Privacy officers • Ethics committees • Data governance teams • Legal departments Follow organizational policies

c. Advocate for Participants

Continue educating decision-makers on:

• Privacy risks • Legal obligations • Ethical responsibilities

d. Follow a Professional Code of Ethics

As a data analyst, it is your responsibility to think beyond management requests.

Your duties include:

• Protecting participant privacy • Maintaining honesty • Preventing misuse of data • Acting in the public interest In conclusion, this scenario has demonstrated how ethical concerns in data science often extend beyond the simple collection and analysis of the data. Although the survey was designed to improve the course and provide management with clear, actionable information, several ethical issues became apparent when the way the data was collected and used was examined. The most egregious concern is the contradiction between requiring participants to log in with their organizational credentials while simultaneously claiming the survey is anonymous. This is a clear disrespect of Spectrum Balance and can undermine trust and create uncertainty about the protection of the participants. Other important ethical considerations include informed consent, transparency, data security, and the potential misuse of information. The participants have the right to understand what information is being collected, how it will be used, who has access to it, and how long it will be stored. If there is no clear communication, participants may feel pressured to provide dishonest responses, undermining the ethical integrity and usefulness of the collected data. Additionally, organizations must be aware of re-identification and function creep when data is collected for one purpose and later used for another without the consent or knowledge of those who provided it. As a professional data analyst, responsibility extends beyond simply providing your technical expertise. Data professionals have an ethical and moral obligation to advocate for fairness, privacy, and accountability throughout the data lifecycle. If your employers choose to ignore your legitimate concerns, it is still important to document recommendations, escalate concerns through appropriate channels, and avoid participating in misleading practices. Ultimately, ethical data science is not only about compliance with rules and regulations: it’s about building trust and ensuring the responsible use of data to benefit organizations and individuals equally without causing harm.

I have been a chef for 21 years; this has led to many unique opportunities. From moving to Vancouver from New Brunswick when I was only 20 and had no money to living in most major cities in Canada. Montreal, Toronto, Moncton, Halifax, Victoria among others; Montreal being my favorite.

Soporte de Emoji

La función emojify se puede llamar directamente en las plantillas o Shortcodes en línea.

Para habilitar emoji globalmente, establece enableEmoji en true en la configuración de tu sitio y luego puedes escribir códigos abreviados de emoji directamente en los archivos de contenido; por ejemplo:

.emoji {
  font-family: Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji, NotoColorEmoji, Segoe UI Symbol, Android Emoji, EmojiSymbols;
}

At the completion of a course, participants are given a survey of 10 questions. To perform the survey, participants access a URL in their web browser that is made available for a short period of time and requires that students log in with their username and password for the organization.

The beginning of the survey prompts for the name of the course, but not their name. Instead, the survey description on this page indicates that all answers and the survey itself will remain anonymous.

Executive management wishes to use the results of the survey to determine which courses require redesign or updating. You are the data analyst assigned to this task and are required to provide actionable insights for this purpose to executive management.

Some ethics concepts and terms that may be discussed here include:

•	Privacy

•	Informed Consent

  1. Based on the information provided, what ethical issues are apparent in the design of this survey and in the sample question?
a.	False Anonymity

Participants needed to use their credentials to log in, yet the survey claimed to be anonymous.

    •	Would the system truly be anonymous?
    •	Where is the login information stored?
    •	Would it be possible to link responses back to individuals?

This could be very misleading and violates participant trust.

b.	Lack of Transparency

The participants are never told:

    •	What data is being collected.
    •	Who has access to it.
    •	The length of time it will be stored.
    •	If their login information is retained.

Participants can’t provide proper informed consent if this information isn't presented.

c.	Potential for Response Bias

Students may fear negative outcomes if they criticize a course.

This could cause:

    •	Inflated ratings
    •	Untruthful responses
    •	Lack of clarity and usefulness in the data

d.	Design Bias in the Survey

The questions could be worded in a way that responses could unintentionally steer participants towards certain answers.

Using poorly designed questions like this can lead to misleading data collection.

a.	Data Security

    •	How is the data from the survey stored?
    •	Is it properly encrypted?
    •	Who has access to the data?
    •	What data is being recorded?

If security is weak and more data than needed is collected, personal information could easily be exposed.

b.	Function Creep

The data that is collected could potentially be used to:

    •	Instructor evaluations
    •	Track student performance
    •	Review employee performance

Using data beyond its original intent without consent is unethical.

c.	Re-Identification Risk

Even without names, combinations of information could identify the participants. 

    •	Course name
    •	Submission time
    •	Class size
    •	Demographic information

It can be difficult to guarantee true anonymity.

d.	Lack of Data Retention Policies

    •	No indication of how long the data will be stored
    •	No indication of when it will be deleted
    •	No indication of who will be responsible for deleting it

  1. What recommendations would you make to executive management?

    a. Be Truthful About Anonymity

    Do not claim that the survey is anonymous unless it is technically impossible to identify the participants.

    b. Improve Transparency

    Provide a clear privacy statement that explains:

    •	What data is collected
•	Why this data is collected
•	Who will have access to it
•	How long it will be stored

    c. Separate Authentication from Responses

    Login only verifies eligibility; once verified, the user’s identity is immediately decoupled from their answers.

    d. Limit Access

    A very limited number of authorized personnel should have access to the survey’s raw data.

    e. Establish Retention Policies

    Define:

    •	How long is data stored?	
•	When will it be deleted?
•	Procedures for secure deletion

    f. Report Aggregated Data Results

    Provide summaries instead of individual responses.

    For example:

    92% of the students felt that the course material was current and up to date.

    This is better than exposing individual answers.

  2. If executive management rejects your recommendations and insists there are no issues, how could you proceed ethically?

    a. Document Your Recommendations and Concerns

    Keep written records of:

    •	Identified risks
•	Recommendations provided
•	Concerns and your reasons for them

    This demonstrates professional due diligence.

    b. Escalate Concerns if Necessary

    Speak with:

    •	Privacy officers
•	Ethics committees
•	Data governance teams
•	Legal departments

    Follow organizational policies

    c. Advocate for Participants

    Continue educating decision-makers on:

    •	Privacy risks
•	Legal obligations
•	Ethical responsibilities

    d. Follow a Professional Code of Ethics

    As a data analyst, it is your responsibility to think beyond management requests.

    Your duties include:

    •	Protecting participant privacy
•	Maintaining honesty
•	Preventing misuse of data
•	Acting in the public interest

    In conclusion, this scenario has demonstrated how ethical concerns in data science often extend beyond the simple collection and analysis of the data. Although the survey was designed to improve the course and provide management with clear, actionable information, several ethical issues became apparent when the way the data was collected and used was examined. The most egregious concern is the contradiction between requiring participants to log in with their organizational credentials while simultaneously claiming the survey is anonymous. This is a clear disrespect of Spectrum Balance and can undermine trust and create uncertainty about the protection of the participants.

    Other important ethical considerations include informed consent, transparency, data security, and the potential misuse of information. The participants have the right to understand what information is being collected, how it will be used, who has access to it, and how long it will be stored. If there is no clear communication, participants may feel pressured to provide dishonest responses, undermining the ethical integrity and usefulness of the collected data. Additionally, organizations must be aware of re-identification and function creep when data is collected for one purpose and later used for another without the consent or knowledge of those who provided it.

    As a professional data analyst, responsibility extends beyond simply providing your technical expertise. Data professionals have an ethical and moral obligation to advocate for fairness, privacy, and accountability throughout the data lifecycle. If your employers choose to ignore your legitimate concerns, it is still important to document recommendations, escalate concerns through appropriate channels, and avoid participating in misleading practices. Ultimately, ethical data science is not only about compliance with rules and regulations: it’s about building trust and ensuring the responsible use of data to benefit organizations and individuals equally without causing harm.

content:
Theoretical Scenario

At the completion of a course, participants are given a survey of 10 questions. To perform the survey, participants access a URL in their web browser that is made available for a short period of time and requires that students log in with their username and password for the organization.

The beginning of the survey prompts for the name of the course, but not their name. Instead, the survey description on this page indicates that all answers and the survey itself will remain anonymous.

Executive management wishes to use the results of the survey to determine which courses require redesign or updating. You are the data analyst assigned to this task and are required to provide actionable insights for this purpose to executive management.

The first question on the survey is shown here:

Figure 1: Example of the first course evaluation question.

Some ethics concepts and terms that may be discussed here include:

•	Privacy
•	Anonymity
•	Informed Consent
•	Accountability
•	Data Minimization
•	Transparency
•	Fairness
•	Bias
•	Trust
  1. Based on the information provided, what ethical issues are apparent in the design of this survey and in the sample question?
a. False Anonymity

Participants needed to use their credentials to log in, yet the survey claimed to be anonymous.

    •	Would the system truly be anonymous?
    •	Where is the login information stored?
    •	Would it be possible to link responses back to individuals?

This could be very misleading and violates participant trust.

b. Lack of Transparency

The participants are never told:

    •	What data is being collected.
    •	Who has access to it.
    •	The length of time it will be stored.
    •	If their login information is retained.

Participants can’t provide proper informed consent if this information isn't presented.

c. Potential for Response Bias

Students may fear negative outcomes if they criticize a course.

This could cause:

    •	Inflated ratings
    •	Untruthful responses
    •	Lack of clarity and usefulness in the data

d. Design Bias in the Survey

The questions could be worded in a way that responses could unintentionally steer participants towards certain answers.

Using poorly designed questions like this can lead to misleading data collection.
  1. What other ethical issues could be present for this survey?
a. Data Security

    •	How is the data from the survey stored?
    •	Is it properly encrypted?
    •	Who has access to the data?
    •	What data is being recorded?

If security is weak and more data than needed is collected, personal information could easily be exposed.

b. Function Creep

The data that is collected could potentially be used to:

    •	Instructor evaluations
    •	Track student performance
    •	Review employee performance

Using data beyond its original intent without consent is unethical.

c. Re-Identification Risk

Even without names, combinations of information could identify the participants. 

    •	Course name
    •	Submission time
    •	Class size
    •	Demographic information

It can be difficult to guarantee true anonymity.

d. Lack of Data Retention Policies

    •	No indication of how long the data will be stored
    •	No indication of when it will be deleted
    •	No indication of who will be responsible for deleting it

  1. What recommendations would you make to executive management?

    a. Be Truthful About Anonymity

    Do not claim that the survey is anonymous unless it is technically impossible to identify the participants.

    b. Improve Transparency

    Provide a clear privacy statement that explains:

     •	What data is collected
 •	Why this data is collected
 •	Who will have access to it
 •	How long it will be stored

    c. Separate Authentication from Responses

    Login only verifies eligibility; once verified, the user’s identity is immediately decoupled from their answers.

    d. Limit Access

    A very limited number of authorized personnel should have access to the survey’s raw data.

    e. Establish Retention Policies

    Define:

     •	How long is data stored?	
 •	When will it be deleted?
 •	Procedures for secure deletion

    f. Report Aggregated Data Results

    Provide summaries instead of individual responses.

    For example:

     92% of the students felt that the course material was current and up to date.

    This is better than exposing individual answers.

  2. If executive management rejects your recommendations and insists there are no issues, how could you proceed ethically?

    a. Document Your Recommendations and Concerns

    Keep written records of:

    •	Identified risks
•	Recommendations provided
•	Concerns and your reasons for them

    This demonstrates professional due diligence.

    b. Escalate Concerns if Necessary

    Speak with:

    •	Privacy officers
•	Ethics committees
•	Data governance teams
•	Legal departments

    Follow organizational policies

    c. Advocate for Participants

    Continue educating decision-makers on:

    •	Privacy risks
•	Legal obligations
•	Ethical responsibilities

    d. Follow a Professional Code of Ethics

    As a data analyst, it is your responsibility to think beyond management requests.

    Your duties include:

    •	Protecting participant privacy
•	Maintaining honesty
•	Preventing misuse of data
•	Acting in the public interest

    In conclusion, this scenario has demonstrated how ethical concerns in data science often extend beyond the simple collection and analysis of the data. Although the survey was designed to improve the course and provide management with clear, actionable information, several ethical issues became apparent when the way the data was collected and used was examined. The most egregious concern is the contradiction between requiring participants to log in with their organizational credentials while simultaneously claiming the survey is anonymous. This is a clear disrespect of Spectrum Balance and can undermine trust and create uncertainty about the protection of the participants.

    Other important ethical considerations include informed consent, transparency, data security, and the potential misuse of information. The participants have the right to understand what information is being collected, how it will be used, who has access to it, and how long it will be stored. If there is no clear communication, participants may feel pressured to provide dishonest responses, undermining the ethical integrity and usefulness of the collected data. Additionally, organizations must be aware of re-identification and function creep when data is collected for one purpose and later used for another without the consent or knowledge of those who provided it.

    As a professional data analyst, responsibility extends beyond simply providing your technical expertise. Data professionals have an ethical and moral obligation to advocate for fairness, privacy, and accountability throughout the data lifecycle. If your employers choose to ignore your legitimate concerns, it is still important to document recommendations, escalate concerns through appropriate channels, and avoid participating in misleading practices. Ultimately, ethical data science is not only about compliance with rules and regulations: it’s about building trust and ensuring the responsible use of data to benefit organizations and individuals equally without causing harm.

content:
Theoretical Scenario

At the completion of a course, participants are given a survey of 10 questions. To perform the survey, participants access a URL in their web browser that is made available for a short period of time and requires that students log in with their username and password for the organization.

The beginning of the survey prompts for the name of the course, but not their name. Instead, the survey description on this page indicates that all answers and the survey itself will remain anonymous.

Executive management wishes to use the results of the survey to determine which courses require redesign or updating. You are the data analyst assigned to this task and are required to provide actionable insights for this purpose to executive management.

The first question on the survey is shown here:

Figure 1: Example of the first course evaluation question.

Some ethics concepts and terms that may be discussed here include:

Privacy Anonymity Informed Consent Accountability Data Minimization Transparency Fairness Bias Trust

  1. Based on the information provided, what ethical issues are apparent in the design of this survey and in the sample question? a. False Anonymity

Participants needed to use their credentials to log in, yet the survey claimed to be anonymous.

Would the system truly be anonymous? Where is the login information stored? Would it be possible to link responses back to individuals?

This could be very misleading and violates participant trust.

b. Lack of Transparency

The participants are never told:

What data is being collected. Who has access to it. The length of time it will be stored. If their login information is retained.

Participants can’t provide proper informed consent if this information isn’t presented.

c. Potential for Response Bias

Students may fear negative outcomes if they criticize a course.

This could cause:

Inflated ratings Untruthful responses Lack of clarity and usefulness in the data d. Design Bias in the Survey

The questions could be worded in a way that responses could unintentionally steer participants towards certain answers.

Using poorly designed questions like this can lead to misleading data collection.

  1. What other ethical issues could be present for this survey? a. Data Security How is the data from the survey stored? Is it properly encrypted? Who has access to the data? What data is being recorded?

If security is weak and more data than needed is collected, personal information could easily be exposed.

b. Function Creep

The data that is collected could potentially be used to:

Instructor evaluations Track student performance Review employee performance

Using data beyond its original intent without consent is unethical.

c. Re-Identification Risk

Even without names, combinations of information could identify the participants.

Course name Submission time Class size Demographic information

It can be difficult to guarantee true anonymity.

d. Lack of Data Retention Policies No indication of how long the data will be stored No indication of when it will be deleted No indication of who will be responsible for deleting it 3. What recommendations would you make to executive management? a. Be Truthful About Anonymity

Do not claim that the survey is anonymous unless it is technically impossible to identify the participants.

b. Improve Transparency

Provide a clear privacy statement that explains:

What data is collected Why this data is collected Who will have access to it How long it will be stored c. Separate Authentication from Responses

Login only verifies eligibility; once verified, the user’s identity is immediately decoupled from their answers.

d. Limit Access

A very limited number of authorized personnel should have access to the survey’s raw data.

e. Establish Retention Policies

Define:

How long is data stored? When will it be deleted? Procedures for secure deletion f. Report Aggregated Data Results

Provide summaries instead of individual responses.

For example:

92% of the students felt that the course material was current and up to date.

This is better than exposing individual answers.

  1. If executive management rejects your recommendations and insists there are no issues, how could you proceed ethically? a. Document Your Recommendations and Concerns

Keep written records of:

Identified risks Recommendations provided Concerns and your reasons for them

This demonstrates professional due diligence.

b. Escalate Concerns if Necessary

Speak with:

Privacy officers Ethics committees Data governance teams Legal departments

Follow organizational policies.

c. Advocate for Participants

Continue educating decision-makers on:

Privacy risks Legal obligations Ethical responsibilities d. Follow a Professional Code of Ethics

As a data analyst, it is your responsibility to think beyond management requests.

Your duties include:

Protecting participant privacy Maintaining honesty Preventing misuse of data Acting in the public interest Conclusion

In conclusion, this scenario has demonstrated how ethical concerns in data science often extend beyond the simple collection and analysis of the data. Although the survey was designed to improve the course and provide management with clear, actionable information, several ethical issues became apparent when the way the data was collected and used was examined. The most egregious concern is the contradiction between requiring participants to log in with their organizational credentials while simultaneously claiming the survey is anonymous. This is a clear disrespect of Spectrum Balance and can undermine trust and create uncertainty about the protection of the participants.

Other important ethical considerations include informed consent, transparency, data security, and the potential misuse of information. The participants have the right to understand what information is being collected, how it will be used, who has access to it, and how long it will be stored. If there is no clear communication, participants may feel pressured to provide dishonest responses, undermining the ethical integrity and usefulness of the collected data. Additionally, organizations must be aware of re-identification and function creep when data is collected for one purpose and later used for another without the consent or knowledge of those who provided it.

As a professional data analyst, responsibility extends beyond simply providing your technical expertise. Data professionals have an ethical and moral obligation to advocate for fairness, privacy, and accountability throughout the data lifecycle. If your employers choose to ignore your legitimate concerns, it is still important to document recommendations, escalate concerns through appropriate channels, and avoid participating in misleading practices. Ultimately, ethical data science is not only about compliance with rules and regulations: it’s about building trust and ensuring the responsible use of data to benefit organizations and individuals equally without causing harm.

content:
Theoretical Scenario

At the completion of a course, participants are given a survey of 10 questions. To perform the survey, participants access a URL in their web browser that is made available for a short period of time and requires that students log in with their username and password for the organization.

The beginning of the survey prompts for the name of the course, but not their name. Instead, the survey description on this page indicates that all answers and the survey itself will remain anonymous.

Executive management wishes to use the results of the survey to determine which courses require redesign or updating. You are the data analyst assigned to this task and are required to provide actionable insights for this purpose to executive management.

The first question on the survey is shown here:

Figure 1: Example of the first course evaluation question.

Some ethics concepts and terms that may be discussed here include:

•	Privacy
•	Anonymity
•	Informed Consent
•	Accountability
•	Data Minimization
•	Transparency
•	Fairness
•	Bias
•	Trust
  1. Based on the information provided, what ethical issues are apparent in the design of this survey and in the sample question?
a. False Anonymity

Participants needed to use their credentials to log in, yet the survey claimed to be anonymous.

    •	Would the system truly be anonymous?
    •	Where is the login information stored?
    •	Would it be possible to link responses back to individuals?

This could be very misleading and violates participant trust.

b. Lack of Transparency

The participants are never told:

    •	What data is being collected.
    •	Who has access to it.
    •	The length of time it will be stored.
    •	If their login information is retained.

Participants can’t provide proper informed consent if this information isn't presented.

c. Potential for Response Bias

Students may fear negative outcomes if they criticize a course.

This could cause:

    •	Inflated ratings
    •	Untruthful responses
    •	Lack of clarity and usefulness in the data

d. Design Bias in the Survey

The questions could be worded in a way that responses could unintentionally steer participants towards certain answers.

Using poorly designed questions like this can lead to misleading data collection.
  1. What other ethical issues could be present for this survey?
a. Data Security

    •	How is the data from the survey stored?
    •	Is it properly encrypted?
    •	Who has access to the data?
    •	What data is being recorded?

If security is weak and more data than needed is collected, personal information could easily be exposed.

b. Function Creep

The data that is collected could potentially be used to:

    •	Instructor evaluations
    •	Track student performance
    •	Review employee performance

Using data beyond its original intent without consent is unethical.

c. Re-Identification Risk

Even without names, combinations of information could identify the participants. 

    •	Course name
    •	Submission time
    •	Class size
    •	Demographic information

It can be difficult to guarantee true anonymity.

d. Lack of Data Retention Policies

    •	No indication of how long the data will be stored
    •	No indication of when it will be deleted
    •	No indication of who will be responsible for deleting it

  1. What recommendations would you make to executive management?

    a. Be Truthful About Anonymity

    Do not claim that the survey is anonymous unless it is technically impossible to identify the participants.

    b. Improve Transparency

    Provide a clear privacy statement that explains:

     •	What data is collected
 •	Why this data is collected
 •	Who will have access to it
 •	How long it will be stored

    c. Separate Authentication from Responses

    Login only verifies eligibility; once verified, the user’s identity is immediately decoupled from their answers.

    d. Limit Access

    A very limited number of authorized personnel should have access to the survey’s raw data.

    e. Establish Retention Policies

    Define:

     •	How long is data stored?	
 •	When will it be deleted?
 •	Procedures for secure deletion

    f. Report Aggregated Data Results

    Provide summaries instead of individual responses.

    For example:

     92% of the students felt that the course material was current and up to date.

    This is better than exposing individual answers.

  2. If executive management rejects your recommendations and insists there are no issues, how could you proceed ethically?

    a. Document Your Recommendations and Concerns

    Keep written records of:

    •	Identified risks
•	Recommendations provided
•	Concerns and your reasons for them

    This demonstrates professional due diligence.

    b. Escalate Concerns if Necessary

    Speak with:

    •	Privacy officers
•	Ethics committees
•	Data governance teams
•	Legal departments

    Follow organizational policies

    c. Advocate for Participants

    Continue educating decision-makers on:

    •	Privacy risks
•	Legal obligations
•	Ethical responsibilities

    d. Follow a Professional Code of Ethics

    As a data analyst, it is your responsibility to think beyond management requests.

    Your duties include:

    •	Protecting participant privacy
•	Maintaining honesty
•	Preventing misuse of data
•	Acting in the public interest

    In conclusion, this scenario has demonstrated how ethical concerns in data science often extend beyond the simple collection and analysis of the data. Although the survey was designed to improve the course and provide management with clear, actionable information, several ethical issues became apparent when the way the data was collected and used was examined. The most egregious concern is the contradiction between requiring participants to log in with their organizational credentials while simultaneously claiming the survey is anonymous. This is a clear disrespect of Spectrum Balance and can undermine trust and create uncertainty about the protection of the participants.

    Other important ethical considerations include informed consent, transparency, data security, and the potential misuse of information. The participants have the right to understand what information is being collected, how it will be used, who has access to it, and how long it will be stored. If there is no clear communication, participants may feel pressured to provide dishonest responses, undermining the ethical integrity and usefulness of the collected data. Additionally, organizations must be aware of re-identification and function creep when data is collected for one purpose and later used for another without the consent or knowledge of those who provided it.

    As a professional data analyst, responsibility extends beyond simply providing your technical expertise. Data professionals have an ethical and moral obligation to advocate for fairness, privacy, and accountability throughout the data lifecycle. If your employers choose to ignore your legitimate concerns, it is still important to document recommendations, escalate concerns through appropriate channels, and avoid participating in misleading practices. Ultimately, ethical data science is not only about compliance with rules and regulations: it’s about building trust and ensuring the responsible use of data to benefit organizations and individuals equally without causing harm.

Why I Made the Change

Family loss and health issues have made me reevaluate life and the trajectory I would like it to take.

Working in hospitality taught me:

  • Leadership
  • Team management
  • Cost Control
  • Problem Solving

These skills transfer well into analytics.

What I am currently studying:

  • Excel
  • SQL
  • Python
  • Power BI

content:
Theoretical Scenario

At the completion of a course, participants are given a survey of 10 questions. To perform the survey, participants access a URL in their web browser that is made available for a short period of time and requires that students log in with their username and password for the organization.

The beginning of the survey prompts for the name of the course, but not their name. Instead, the survey description on this page indicates that all answers and the survey itself will remain anonymous.

Executive management wishes to use the results of the survey to determine which courses require redesign or updating. You are the data analyst assigned to this task and are required to provide actionable insights for this purpose to executive management.

The first question on the survey is shown here:

Figure 1: Example of the first course evaluation question.

Some ethics concepts and terms that may be discussed here include:

•	Privacy
•	Anonymity
•	Informed Consent
•	Accountability
•	Data Minimization
•	Transparency
•	Fairness
•	Bias
•	Trust
  1. Based on the information provided, what ethical issues are apparent in the design of this survey and in the sample question?
a. False Anonymity

Participants needed to use their credentials to log in, yet the survey claimed to be anonymous.

    •	Would the system truly be anonymous?
    •	Where is the login information stored?
    •	Would it be possible to link responses back to individuals?

This could be very misleading and violates participant trust.

b. Lack of Transparency

The participants are never told:

    •	What data is being collected.
    •	Who has access to it.
    •	The length of time it will be stored.
    •	If their login information is retained.

Participants can’t provide proper informed consent if this information isn't presented.

c. Potential for Response Bias

Students may fear negative outcomes if they criticize a course.

This could cause:

    •	Inflated ratings
    •	Untruthful responses
    •	Lack of clarity and usefulness in the data

d. Design Bias in the Survey

The questions could be worded in a way that responses could unintentionally steer participants towards certain answers.

Using poorly designed questions like this can lead to misleading data collection.
  1. What other ethical issues could be present for this survey?
a. Data Security

    •	How is the data from the survey stored?
    •	Is it properly encrypted?
    •	Who has access to the data?
    •	What data is being recorded?

If security is weak and more data than needed is collected, personal information could easily be exposed.

b. Function Creep

The data that is collected could potentially be used to:

    •	Instructor evaluations
    •	Track student performance
    •	Review employee performance

Using data beyond its original intent without consent is unethical.

c. Re-Identification Risk

Even without names, combinations of information could identify the participants. 

    •	Course name
    •	Submission time
    •	Class size
    •	Demographic information

It can be difficult to guarantee true anonymity.

d. Lack of Data Retention Policies

    •	No indication of how long the data will be stored
    •	No indication of when it will be deleted
    •	No indication of who will be responsible for deleting it

  1. What recommendations would you make to executive management?

    a. Be Truthful About Anonymity

    Do not claim that the survey is anonymous unless it is technically impossible to identify the participants.

    b. Improve Transparency

    Provide a clear privacy statement that explains:

     •	What data is collected
 •	Why this data is collected
 •	Who will have access to it
 •	How long it will be stored

    c. Separate Authentication from Responses

    Login only verifies eligibility; once verified, the user’s identity is immediately decoupled from their answers.

    d. Limit Access

    A very limited number of authorized personnel should have access to the survey’s raw data.

    e. Establish Retention Policies

    Define:

     •	How long is data stored?	
 •	When will it be deleted?
 •	Procedures for secure deletion

    f. Report Aggregated Data Results

    Provide summaries instead of individual responses.

    For example:

     92% of the students felt that the course material was current and up to date.

    This is better than exposing individual answers.

  2. If executive management rejects your recommendations and insists there are no issues, how could you proceed ethically?

    a. Document Your Recommendations and Concerns

    Keep written records of:

    •	Identified risks
•	Recommendations provided
•	Concerns and your reasons for them

    This demonstrates professional due diligence.

    b. Escalate Concerns if Necessary

    Speak with:

    •	Privacy officers
•	Ethics committees
•	Data governance teams
•	Legal departments

    Follow organizational policies

    c. Advocate for Participants

    Continue educating decision-makers on:

    •	Privacy risks
•	Legal obligations
•	Ethical responsibilities

    d. Follow a Professional Code of Ethics

    As a data analyst, it is your responsibility to think beyond management requests.

    Your duties include:

    •	Protecting participant privacy
•	Maintaining honesty
•	Preventing misuse of data
•	Acting in the public interest

    In conclusion, this scenario has demonstrated how ethical concerns in data science often extend beyond the simple collection and analysis of the data. Although the survey was designed to improve the course and provide management with clear, actionable information, several ethical issues became apparent when the way the data was collected and used was examined. The most egregious concern is the contradiction between requiring participants to log in with their organizational credentials while simultaneously claiming the survey is anonymous. This is a clear disrespect of Spectrum Balance and can undermine trust and create uncertainty about the protection of the participants.

    Other important ethical considerations include informed consent, transparency, data security, and the potential misuse of information. The participants have the right to understand what information is being collected, how it will be used, who has access to it, and how long it will be stored. If there is no clear communication, participants may feel pressured to provide dishonest responses, undermining the ethical integrity and usefulness of the collected data. Additionally, organizations must be aware of re-identification and function creep when data is collected for one purpose and later used for another without the consent or knowledge of those who provided it.

    As a professional data analyst, responsibility extends beyond simply providing your technical expertise. Data professionals have an ethical and moral obligation to advocate for fairness, privacy, and accountability throughout the data lifecycle. If your employers choose to ignore your legitimate concerns, it is still important to document recommendations, escalate concerns through appropriate channels, and avoid participating in misleading practices. Ultimately, ethical data science is not only about compliance with rules and regulations: it’s about building trust and ensuring the responsible use of data to benefit organizations and individuals equally without causing harm.

Las ecuaciones matemáticas se pueden renderizar usando la sintaxis de Mathjax con soporte de símbolos AMS.

Opcionalmente, habilita esto por página agregando mathjax: true a tu frontmatter.

Luego, usa $$ ... $$ en una línea por sí sola para renderizar una ecuación de bloque:

$$ | Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{1}} [A(x) = 1] - Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{2}} [A(x) = 1] | < \text{negligible} $$

La versión sin procesar es:

$$ | Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{1}} [A(x) = 1] - Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{2}} [A(x) = 1] | < \text{negligible} $$

Escribe ecuaciones en línea con \\( ... \\) , como \( x^n / y \) . ¡Es fácil!

Los emoji se pueden habilitar en un proyecto Hugo de varias maneras. :zap:

Soporte de Emoji

La función emojify se puede llamar directamente en las plantillas o Shortcodes en línea.

Para habilitar emoji globalmente, establece enableEmoji en true en la configuración de tu sitio y luego puedes escribir códigos abreviados de emoji directamente en los archivos de contenido; por ejemplo:

La Hoja de trucos de Emoji es una referencia útil para los códigos abreviados de emoji.

N.B. Los pasos anteriores habilitan los caracteres y secuencias de emoji del Estándar Unicode en Hugo, sin embargo, la representación de estos glifos depende del navegador y la plataforma. Para estilizar los emoji, puedes usar una fuente de emoji de terceros o una pila de fuentes; por ejemplo:

.emoji {
  font-family: Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji, NotoColorEmoji, Segoe UI Symbol, Android Emoji, EmojiSymbols;
}

.emoji {

content:
Theoretical Scenario

At the completion of a course, participants are given a survey of 10 questions. To perform the survey, participants access a URL in their web browser that is made available for a short period of time and requires that students log in with their username and password for the organization.

The beginning of the survey prompts for the name of the course, but not their name. Instead, the survey description on this page indicates that all answers and the survey itself will remain anonymous.

Executive management wishes to use the results of the survey to determine which courses require redesign or updating. You are the data analyst assigned to this task and are required to provide actionable insights for this purpose to executive management.

The first question on the survey is shown here:

Figure 1: Example of the first course evaluation question.

Some ethics concepts and terms that may be discussed here include:

•	Privacy
•	Anonymity
•	Informed Consent
•	Accountability
•	Data Minimization
•	Transparency
•	Fairness
•	Bias
•	Trust

1. Based on the information provided, what ethical issues are apparent in the design of this survey and in the sample question?

a. False Anonymity

Participants needed to use their credentials to log in, yet the survey claimed to be anonymous.

    •	Would the system truly be anonymous?
    •	Where is the login information stored?
    •	Would it be possible to link responses back to individuals?

This could be very misleading and violates participant trust.

b. Lack of Transparency

The participants are never told:

    •	What data is being collected.
    •	Who has access to it.
    •	The length of time it will be stored.
    •	If their login information is retained.

Participants can’t provide proper informed consent if this information isn't presented.

c. Potential for Response Bias

Students may fear negative outcomes if they criticize a course.

This could cause:

    •	Inflated ratings
    •	Untruthful responses
    •	Lack of clarity and usefulness in the data

d. Design Bias in the Survey

The questions could be worded in a way that responses could unintentionally steer participants towards certain answers.

Using poorly designed questions like this can lead to misleading data collection.
  1. What other ethical issues could be present for this survey?
a. Data Security

    •	How is the data from the survey stored?
    •	Is it properly encrypted?
    •	Who has access to the data?
    •	What data is being recorded?

If security is weak and more data than needed is collected, personal information could easily be exposed.

b. Function Creep

The data that is collected could potentially be used to:

    •	Instructor evaluations
    •	Track student performance
    •	Review employee performance

Using data beyond its original intent without consent is unethical.

c. Re-Identification Risk

Even without names, combinations of information could identify the participants. 

    •	Course name
    •	Submission time
    •	Class size
    •	Demographic information

It can be difficult to guarantee true anonymity.

d. Lack of Data Retention Policies

    •	No indication of how long the data will be stored
    •	No indication of when it will be deleted
    •	No indication of who will be responsible for deleting it

3. What recommendations would you make to executive management?

a. Be Truthful About Anonymity

Do not claim that the survey is anonymous unless it is technically impossible to identify the participants.

b. Improve Transparency

Provide a clear privacy statement that explains:
    
    •	What data is collected
    •	Why this data is collected
    •	Who will have access to it
    •	How long it will be stored

c. Separate Authentication from Responses

Login only verifies eligibility; once verified, the user's identity is immediately decoupled from their answers.

d. Limit Access

A very limited number of authorized personnel should have access to the survey's raw data.

e. Establish Retention Policies

Define:

    •	How long is data stored?	
    •	When will it be deleted?
    •	Procedures for secure deletion

f. Report Aggregated Data Results

Provide summaries instead of individual responses.

For example:

	92% of the students felt that the course material was current and up to date.

This is better than exposing individual answers.

  1. If executive management rejects your recommendations and insists there are no issues, how could you proceed ethically?

    a. Document Your Recommendations and Concerns

    Keep written records of:

    •	Identified risks
•	Recommendations provided
•	Concerns and your reasons for them

    This demonstrates professional due diligence.

    b. Escalate Concerns if Necessary

    Speak with:

    •	Privacy officers
•	Ethics committees
•	Data governance teams
•	Legal departments

    Follow organizational policies

    c. Advocate for Participants

    Continue educating decision-makers on:

    •	Privacy risks
•	Legal obligations
•	Ethical responsibilities

    d. Follow a Professional Code of Ethics

    As a data analyst, it is your responsibility to think beyond management requests.

    Your duties include:

    •	Protecting participant privacy
•	Maintaining honesty
•	Preventing misuse of data
•	Acting in the public interest

    In conclusion, this scenario has demonstrated how ethical concerns in data science often extend beyond the simple collection and analysis of the data. Although the survey was designed to improve the course and provide management with clear, actionable information, several ethical issues became apparent when the way the data was collected and used was examined. The most egregious concern is the contradiction between requiring participants to log in with their organizational credentials while simultaneously claiming the survey is anonymous. This is a clear disrespect of Spectrum Balance and can undermine trust and create uncertainty about the protection of the participants.

    Other important ethical considerations include informed consent, transparency, data security, and the potential misuse of information. The participants have the right to understand what information is being collected, how it will be used, who has access to it, and how long it will be stored. If there is no clear communication, participants may feel pressured to provide dishonest responses, undermining the ethical integrity and usefulness of the collected data. Additionally, organizations must be aware of re-identification and function creep when data is collected for one purpose and later used for another without the consent or knowledge of those who provided it.

    As a professional data analyst, responsibility extends beyond simply providing your technical expertise. Data professionals have an ethical and moral obligation to advocate for fairness, privacy, and accountability throughout the data lifecycle. If your employers choose to ignore your legitimate concerns, it is still important to document recommendations, escalate concerns through appropriate channels, and avoid participating in misleading practices. Ultimately, ethical data science is not only about compliance with rules and regulations: it’s about building trust and ensuring the responsible use of data to benefit organizations and individuals equally without causing harm.

.emoji {

}

content:
Theoretical Scenario

At the completion of a course, participants are given a survey of 10 questions. To perform the survey, participants access a URL in their web browser that is made available for a short period of time and requires that students log in with their username and password for the organization.

The beginning of the survey prompts for the name of the course, but not their name. Instead, the survey description on this page indicates that all answers and the survey itself will remain anonymous.

Executive management wishes to use the results of the survey to determine which courses require redesign or updating. You are the data analyst assigned to this task and are required to provide actionable insights for this purpose to executive management.

The first question on the survey is shown here:

Figure 1: Example of the first course evaluation question.

Some ethics concepts and terms that may be discussed here include:

•	Privacy
•	Anonymity
•	Informed Consent
•	Accountability
•	Data Minimization
•	Transparency
•	Fairness
•	Bias
•	Trust

1. Based on the information provided, what ethical issues are apparent in the design of this survey and in the sample question?

a. False Anonymity

Participants needed to use their credentials to log in, yet the survey claimed to be anonymous.

    •	Would the system truly be anonymous?
    •	Where is the login information stored?
    •	Would it be possible to link responses back to individuals?

This could be very misleading and violates participant trust.

b. Lack of Transparency

The participants are never told:

    •	What data is being collected.
    •	Who has access to it.
    •	The length of time it will be stored.
    •	If their login information is retained.

Participants can’t provide proper informed consent if this information isn't presented.

c. Potential for Response Bias

Students may fear negative outcomes if they criticize a course.

This could cause:

    •	Inflated ratings
    •	Untruthful responses
    •	Lack of clarity and usefulness in the data

d. Design Bias in the Survey

The questions could be worded in a way that responses could unintentionally steer participants towards certain answers.

Using poorly designed questions like this can lead to misleading data collection.

2. What other ethical issues could be present for this survey?

a. Data Security

    •	How is the data from the survey stored?
    •	Is it properly encrypted?
    •	Who has access to the data?
    •	What data is being recorded?

If security is weak and more data than needed is collected, personal information could easily be exposed.

b. Function Creep

The data that is collected could potentially be used to:

    •	Instructor evaluations
    •	Track student performance
    •	Review employee performance

Using data beyond its original intent without consent is unethical.

c. Re-Identification Risk

Even without names, combinations of information could identify the participants. 

    •	Course name
    •	Submission time
    •	Class size
    •	Demographic information

It can be difficult to guarantee true anonymity.

d. Lack of Data Retention Policies

    •	No indication of how long the data will be stored
    •	No indication of when it will be deleted
    •	No indication of who will be responsible for deleting it

3. What recommendations would you make to executive management?

a. Be Truthful About Anonymity

Do not claim that the survey is anonymous unless it is technically impossible to identify the participants.

b. Improve Transparency

Provide a clear privacy statement that explains:
    
    •	What data is collected
    •	Why this data is collected
    •	Who will have access to it
    •	How long it will be stored

c. Separate Authentication from Responses

Login only verifies eligibility; once verified, the user's identity is immediately decoupled from their answers.

d. Limit Access

A very limited number of authorized personnel should have access to the survey's raw data.

e. Establish Retention Policies

Define:

    •	How long is data stored?	
    •	When will it be deleted?
    •	Procedures for secure deletion

f. Report Aggregated Data Results

Provide summaries instead of individual responses.

For example:

	92% of the students felt that the course material was current and up to date.

This is better than exposing individual answers.

4. If executive management rejects your recommendations and insists there are no issues, how could you proceed ethically?

a.	Document Your Recommendations and Concerns

Keep written records of:

    •	Identified risks
    •	Recommendations provided
    •	Concerns and your reasons for them

This demonstrates professional due diligence.

b.	Escalate Concerns if Necessary

Speak with:

    •	Privacy officers
    •	Ethics committees
    •	Data governance teams
    •	Legal departments 

Follow organizational policies

c.	Advocate for Participants

Continue educating decision-makers on:

    •	Privacy risks
    •	Legal obligations
    •	Ethical responsibilities

d.	Follow a Professional Code of Ethics

As a data analyst, it is your responsibility to think beyond management requests.

Your duties include:

    •	Protecting participant privacy
    •	Maintaining honesty
    •	Preventing misuse of data
    •	Acting in the public interest

In conclusion, this scenario has demonstrated how ethical concerns in data science often extend beyond the simple collection and analysis of the data. Although the survey was designed to improve the course and provide management with clear, actionable information, several ethical issues became apparent when the way the data was collected and used was examined. The most egregious concern is the contradiction between requiring participants to log in with their organizational credentials while simultaneously claiming the survey is anonymous. This is a clear disrespect of Spectrum Balance and can undermine trust and create uncertainty about the protection of the participants.

Other important ethical considerations include informed consent, transparency, data security, and the potential misuse of information.  The participants have the right to understand what information is being collected, how it will be used, who has access to it, and how long it will be stored. If there is no clear communication, participants may feel pressured to provide dishonest responses, undermining the ethical integrity and usefulness of the collected data. Additionally, organizations must be aware of re-identification and function creep when data is collected for one purpose and later used for another without the consent or knowledge of those who provided it.

As a professional data analyst, responsibility extends beyond simply providing your technical expertise. Data professionals have an ethical and moral obligation to advocate for fairness, privacy, and accountability throughout the data lifecycle. If your employers choose to ignore your legitimate concerns, it is still important to document recommendations, escalate concerns through appropriate channels, and avoid participating in misleading practices. Ultimately, ethical data science is not only about compliance with rules and regulations: it’s about building trust and ensuring the responsible use of data to benefit organizations and individuals equally without causing harm.

Los emoji se pueden habilitar en un proyecto Hugo de varias maneras. :zap:

Soporte de Emoji

La función emojify se puede llamar directamente en las plantillas o Shortcodes en línea.

Para habilitar emoji globalmente, establece enableEmoji en true en la configuración de tu sitio y luego puedes escribir códigos abreviados de emoji directamente en los archivos de contenido; por ejemplo:

La Hoja de trucos de Emoji es una referencia útil para los códigos abreviados de emoji.

N.B. Los pasos anteriores habilitan los caracteres y secuencias de emoji del Estándar Unicode en Hugo, sin embargo, la representación de estos glifos depende del navegador y la plataforma. Para estilizar los emoji, puedes usar una fuente de emoji de terceros o una pila de fuentes; por ejemplo:

.emoji {
  font-family: Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji, NotoColorEmoji, Segoe UI Symbol, Android Emoji, EmojiSymbols;
}

content:
Theoretical Scenario

At the completion of a course, participants are given a survey of 10 questions. To perform the survey, participants access a URL in their web browser that is made available for a short period of time and requires that students log in with their username and password for the organization.

The beginning of the survey prompts for the name of the course, but not their name. Instead, the survey description on this page indicates that all answers and the survey itself will remain anonymous.

Executive management wishes to use the results of the survey to determine which courses require redesign or updating. You are the data analyst assigned to this task and are required to provide actionable insights for this purpose to executive management.

The first question on the survey is shown here:

Figure 1: Example of the first course evaluation question.

Some ethics concepts and terms that may be discussed here include:

•	Privacy
•	Anonymity
•	Informed Consent
•	Accountability
•	Data Minimization
•	Transparency
•	Fairness
•	Bias
•	Trust

1. Based on the information provided, what ethical issues are apparent in the design of this survey and in the sample question?

a. False Anonymity

Participants needed to use their credentials to log in, yet the survey claimed to be anonymous.

    •	Would the system truly be anonymous?
    •	Where is the login information stored?
    •	Would it be possible to link responses back to individuals?

This could be very misleading and violates participant trust.

b. Lack of Transparency

The participants are never told:

    •	What data is being collected.
    •	Who has access to it.
    •	The length of time it will be stored.
    •	If their login information is retained.

Participants can’t provide proper informed consent if this information isn't presented.

c. Potential for Response Bias

Students may fear negative outcomes if they criticize a course.

This could cause:

    •	Inflated ratings
    •	Untruthful responses
    •	Lack of clarity and usefulness in the data

d. Design Bias in the Survey

The questions could be worded in a way that responses could unintentionally steer participants towards certain answers.

Using poorly designed questions like this can lead to misleading data collection.

2. What other ethical issues could be present for this survey?

a. Data Security

    •	How is the data from the survey stored?
    •	Is it properly encrypted?
    •	Who has access to the data?
    •	What data is being recorded?

If security is weak and more data than needed is collected, personal information could easily be exposed.

b. Function Creep

The data that is collected could potentially be used to:

    •	Instructor evaluations
    •	Track student performance
    •	Review employee performance

Using data beyond its original intent without consent is unethical.

c. Re-Identification Risk

Even without names, combinations of information could identify the participants. 

    •	Course name
    •	Submission time
    •	Class size
    •	Demographic information

It can be difficult to guarantee true anonymity.

d. Lack of Data Retention Policies

    •	No indication of how long the data will be stored
    •	No indication of when it will be deleted
    •	No indication of who will be responsible for deleting it

3. What recommendations would you make to executive management?

a. Be Truthful About Anonymity

Do not claim that the survey is anonymous unless it is technically impossible to identify the participants.

b. Improve Transparency

Provide a clear privacy statement that explains:
    
    •	What data is collected
    •	Why this data is collected
    •	Who will have access to it
    •	How long it will be stored

c. Separate Authentication from Responses

Login only verifies eligibility; once verified, the user's identity is immediately decoupled from their answers.

d. Limit Access

A very limited number of authorized personnel should have access to the survey's raw data.

e. Establish Retention Policies

Define:

    •	How long is data stored?	
    •	When will it be deleted?
    •	Procedures for secure deletion

f. Report Aggregated Data Results

Provide summaries instead of individual responses.

For example:

	92% of the students felt that the course material was current and up to date.

This is better than exposing individual answers.

4. If executive management rejects your recommendations and insists there are no issues, how could you proceed ethically?

a.	Document Your Recommendations and Concerns

Keep written records of:

    •	Identified risks
    •	Recommendations provided
    •	Concerns and your reasons for them

This demonstrates professional due diligence.

b.	Escalate Concerns if Necessary

Speak with:

    •	Privacy officers
    •	Ethics committees
    •	Data governance teams
    •	Legal departments 

Follow organizational policies

c.	Advocate for Participants

Continue educating decision-makers on:

    •	Privacy risks
    •	Legal obligations
    •	Ethical responsibilities

d.	Follow a Professional Code of Ethics

As a data analyst, it is your responsibility to think beyond management requests.

Your duties include:

    •	Protecting participant privacy
    •	Maintaining honesty
    •	Preventing misuse of data
    •	Acting in the public interest

In conclusion, this scenario has demonstrated how ethical concerns in data science often extend beyond the simple collection and analysis of the data. Although the survey was designed to improve the course and provide management with clear, actionable information, several ethical issues became apparent when the way the data was collected and used was examined. The most egregious concern is the contradiction between requiring participants to log in with their organizational credentials while simultaneously claiming the survey is anonymous. This is a clear disrespect of Spectrum Balance and can undermine trust and create uncertainty about the protection of the participants.

Other important ethical considerations include informed consent, transparency, data security, and the potential misuse of information.  The participants have the right to understand what information is being collected, how it will be used, who has access to it, and how long it will be stored. If there is no clear communication, participants may feel pressured to provide dishonest responses, undermining the ethical integrity and usefulness of the collected data. Additionally, organizations must be aware of re-identification and function creep when data is collected for one purpose and later used for another without the consent or knowledge of those who provided it.

As a professional data analyst, responsibility extends beyond simply providing your technical expertise. Data professionals have an ethical and moral obligation to advocate for fairness, privacy, and accountability throughout the data lifecycle. If your employers choose to ignore your legitimate concerns, it is still important to document recommendations, escalate concerns through appropriate channels, and avoid participating in misleading practices. Ultimately, ethical data science is not only about compliance with rules and regulations: it’s about building trust and ensuring the responsible use of data to benefit organizations and individuals equally without causing harm.
title: Ethical Perspectives: A Data Analysis

My Journey as a Chef

I have been a chef for 21 years; this has led to many unique opportunities. From moving to Vancouver from New Brunswick when I was only 20 and had no money to living in most major cities in Canada. Montreal, Toronto, Moncton, Halifax, Victoria among others; Montreal being my favorite.

I even ended up in the Caribbean for a period! Beautiful place, but I don’t suggest living there unless you’re a millionaire! This has given me a wide variety of skills and experiences, which led to the ownership of my own restaurant for a time. However, it didn’t work out but it gave me valuable career experience.

Why I Made the Change

Family loss and health issues have made me reevaluate life and the trajectory I would like it to take.

Working in hospitality taught me:

  • Leadership
  • Team management
  • Cost Control
  • Problem Solving

These skills transfer well into analytics.

What I am currently studying:

  • Excel
  • SQL
  • Python
  • Power BI
  • Data Visualization

Looking Ahead

My goal is to combine my hospitality knowledge and experience with my studies in data analytics to help businesses make better decisions.
title: My Journey from Chef to Data Analyst

Las ecuaciones matemáticas se pueden renderizar usando la sintaxis de Mathjax con soporte de símbolos AMS.

Opcionalmente, habilita esto por página agregando mathjax: true a tu frontmatter.

Luego, usa $$ ... $$ en una línea por sí sola para renderizar una ecuación de bloque:

$$ | Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{1}} [A(x) = 1] - Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{2}} [A(x) = 1] | < \text{negligible} $$

La versión sin procesar es:

$$ | Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{1}} [A(x) = 1] - Pr_{x \leftarrow P_{2}} [A(x) = 1] | < \text{negligible} $$

Escribe ecuaciones en línea con \\( ... \\) , como \( x^n / y \) . ¡Es fácil!

Los emoji se pueden habilitar en un proyecto Hugo de varias maneras. :zap:

Soporte de Emoji

La función emojify se puede llamar directamente en las plantillas o Shortcodes en línea.

Para habilitar emoji globalmente, establece enableEmoji en true en la configuración de tu sitio y luego puedes escribir códigos abreviados de emoji directamente en los archivos de contenido; por ejemplo:

La Hoja de trucos de Emoji es una referencia útil para los códigos abreviados de emoji.

N.B. Los pasos anteriores habilitan los caracteres y secuencias de emoji del Estándar Unicode en Hugo, sin embargo, la representación de estos glifos depende del navegador y la plataforma. Para estilizar los emoji, puedes usar una fuente de emoji de terceros o una pila de fuentes; por ejemplo:

.emoji {
  font-family: Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji, NotoColorEmoji, Segoe UI Symbol, Android Emoji, EmojiSymbols;
}
